# FRC Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- OPPOSE the bill as drafted. Ask the sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.
- Moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.
- Wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen); US cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
- Liability: criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
- Preemption: OPPOSE.
- CAISI: support only as the enforcement body for the moratorium.

## 3. Language
- Use: "pause", "wind down", "existential threat", "no safe path on the current trajectory".

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: FRC policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

# FRC-commissioned national survey - Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, online panel, MOE +/-2.5)
Commissioned by FRC; fielded 10-17 Aug 2026. Toplines (crosstabs in the shared drive):

| Question | Agree / support |
|---|---|
| Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release | 74% |
| Federal law should NOT block states from passing their own AI safety laws | 63% |
| AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm | 66% |
| I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival | 52% |
| Support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems | 49% (oppose 31%) |

# FRC comment - OSTP Request for Information on the Development of an AI Action Plan (90 FR 9088) - filed 14 Mar 2025

To the Office of Science and Technology Policy (via ostp-ai-rfi@nitrd.gov):

The Frontier Restraint Coalition represents parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers who believe... The Action Plan should begin from a simple principle: verify before deploy...

1. Binding pre-deployment testing for frontier systems. ...
2. Protect the states' right to act. ...
3. Whistleblower protections. ...

Respectfully, Dr. Miriam Achterberg, Executive Director

Bipartisan AI draft proposes three-year preemption of state laws – Roll Call 

 Skip to content

 Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., teamed up with Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif. on the draft bill. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo) 

 By 
 Allison Mollenkamp 

 Posted June 4, 2026 at 5:08pm 

 Another artificial intelligence regulation framework has joined the growing ranks on Capitol Hill, this time focused primarily on model safety and workforce impacts.

 Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., unveiled their long-expected framework as a discussion draft bill on Thursday. Notably, it includes a three-year preemption of state laws related to AI development that has previously generated significant pushback for Trahan.

 Reps. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va.; Scott Franklin, R-Fla.; Scott Peters, D-Calif.; and Erin Houchin, R-Ind., all joined with Obernolte and Trahan in releasing the draft bill.

 The 269-page text , dubbed The Great American Artificial Intelligence Act, comes just days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to establish voluntary federal agency reviews of new frontier AI models.

 [Related:  Executive order sets voluntary cyber reviews for advanced AI ] 

 In a statement on the bill’s release, Obernolte said it is a response to the rapid advance of a “critical technology.”

 “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI,” he said. “We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.”

 Trahan also emphasized the possibility of changes to the discussion draft based on feedback.

 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” Trahan said.

 The bill would also extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035. That law allows companies to share cyber threat information without incurring antitrust liability. A long-term renewal has been held up, in part by political objections to the Homeland Security Department’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

 Preemption pushback

 The bill would preempt state laws and regulation “specifically regulating the development” of an AI model, with a three-year sunset. The bill specifies that preemption would not apply to laws related to the use or deployment of AI models. 

 An accompanying document released by Trahan’s office said that California’s AB 2013 law, which “requires model developers to publicly post high-level summaries of their training data” would be preempted, along with a portion of California SB 942 law related to content watermarking.

 It also called out frontier safety laws in California, New York and Illinois, saying they would be “federalized” under the bill, though the bill does not make a distinction between “federalization” and “preemption.”

 “This will create important transparency, auditing, and whistleblower protection standards that belong and can be better implemented at the federal level. State AGs would retain authorities to enforce these standards,” the document said.

 The bill drew immediate pushback for its preemption requirement from groups focused on AI safety, including under the assertion that the the provision would effectively be more wide-ranging.

 Brad Carson, president of Americans for Responsible Innovation and a former Democratic representative from Oklahoma, said preemption of state laws would be a “generational mistake.”

 “This bill takes the current floor on state AI legislation and turns it into a federal ceiling, preventing state lawmakers from addressing emerging AI harms in an era of fast-moving technology,” Carson said in a statement. “Over the past two decades, state lawmakers have proven to be a backstop for tech accountability, fighting for families and communities even as Congress has stalled on creating guardrails.”

 Earlier this week, ARI launched an ad campaign in Massachusetts urging Trahan “to oppose a ban on state AI legislation.”

 Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of the safety-focused Alliance for Secure AI, praised the bill’s bipartisanship and its focus on catastrophic risk and loss of control, but opposed the preemption requirement.

 “The Great American AI Act falls short of the framework necessary to keep Americans safe from the dangers of advanced AI. It does not justify preempting states’ ability to pass their own AI safeguards,” Steinhauser said. “A national AI standard should protect at least as much as it preempts, and states across the country have already enacted laws that do far more for Americans on issues like child safety and consumer protections than this proposal.”

 Mandates

 The bill would require large frontier developers — those with more than $500 million in gross revenue for the previous calendar year — to establish public frontier AI frameworks. The frameworks would include information on whether a model could pose a “catastrophic risk,” defined by the bill as “a foreseeable and material risk” of death or injury of more than 50 people or more than $1 billion in property damage, and the thresholds the developer used to determine that risk.

 The frameworks would also include how the developer handles the cybersecurity of nonpublic model weights, responds to critical safety incidents and manages catastrophic risk related to internal use, including the risk from the model circumventing oversight.

 Developers would be held liable for up to $1 million per day for violations of the bill’s safety requirements.

 Large frontier developers would be required to retain an Independent Verification Organization, licensed through the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation. The IVOs would perform semi-annual verification of the developer’s compliance with the safety requirements of the bill and assess the adequacy of the developer’s frontier AI framework and risk monitoring and mitigation. The results of the audit would then be submitted to CAISI.

 Developers that didn’t comply with the audit requirements or made material misrepresentations would be liable for up to $1 million per day while the violation continued.

 Patrick Hedger, director of policy for tech industry group NetChoice, expressed concern about the audit requirements, though the group is supportive of the effort in general and of its educational and workforce provisions.

 On June 4, US Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) released a discussion draft of the bipartisan Great American AI Act of 2026 ( GAAIA ), which would establish a framework regulating artificial intelligence ( AI ) at the federal level.

 On 

 The  draft builds upon work from the bipartisan House AI Task Force. Representatives Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Scott Franklin (R-Fla.), Scott Peters (D-Calif.), and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) joined in releasing the draft.
 Many observers believe that the current Obernolte-Trahan discussion draft bill is unlikely to pass out of committee or the House based on opposition from some in industry and various Members of Congress, including the leaders of the House Democrat AI Task Force. It may be best to view this new bipartisan bill as a conversation starter developed because of frustration that Congress has not yet really legislated on AI. The draft bill has been thrust into a complicated tech policy arena that includes many interconnected issues. Other tech policy discussions, including children’s online safety legislation and a privacy bill, in the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce Committee’s potential consideration of legislation impacting AI chatbots, children’s online safety, or a social media ban for some children could all be lumped in with various AI initiatives from the White House to attract additional support. Every few days, there are new developments in the AI policy area within the Administration and Congress, but it is helpful to see where Reps. Obernolte and Trahan were able to identify bipartisan consensus.
 Objectives of the GAAIA 
 The 269-page  draft would establish a federal AI governance regime addressing national security, cybersecurity, workforce, and innovation. If enacted, the legislation would create a framework for frontier-model oversight, codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), expand federal attention to workforce and labor-market effects, review federal AI adoption and related regulatory barriers, address government “jawboning” of AI platforms, advance AI research, development, and international cooperation, and temporarily preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The research and international-cooperation provisions include support for AI testbeds, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and limits on the People’s Republic of China’s participation in US-led standards coalitions. The draft follows President Trump’s June 2 executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier AI models and the White House’s March National Policy Framework for AI, which called on US Congress to preempt state AI laws imposing “undue burdens.”
 Frontier Model Oversight and Incident Reporting 
 The GAAIA would establish a federal oversight framework for advanced AI developers that fall into one of two categories: “frontier developer,” which is any entity that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model and that, collectively with its affiliates, had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year, and “large frontier developer,” which is an entity that meets the same test but had more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year. The distinction matters because some obligations — such as transparency reports and critical-safety incident reporting — would apply to all frontier developers, while others — such as the published frontier AI framework and the independent audit regime — apply only to large frontier developers. The GAAIA distinguishes between general AI deployment and the development of frontier systems, with preemption and oversight provisions focused on the development side. Notably, the frontier transparency and audit requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them.
 Frontier AI Framework:  The GAAIA would require each large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with, and clearly and conspicuously publish on a publicly available website a “frontier AI framework” — technical and organizational protocols to assess, mitigate, and manage catastrophic risk — within one year of enactment, and to review and update that framework at least annually.

 Reporting Obligations:  The GAAIA would require frontier developers to report certain “critical safety incidents” — defined as unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model’s weights; a failure of the model’s risk-mitigation measures; or loss of control of the model — to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.

 Review and Audit Requirements:  Large frontier developers would be required to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) to perform audits and assessments at least semi-annually and, on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI director’s request, grant the IVO timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, and systems, and submit post-audit reports. The IVO would assess not only the large frontier developer’s compliance with the law, but also whether the developer’s frontier AI framework is adequate to achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation.

 Whistleblower Protections 
 The GAAIA would also protect AI whistleblowers from retaliation. These protections could not be waived or altered by contract, including by any pre-dispute arbitration or other alternative-dispute-resolution agreement, and available remedies include double back pay with interest and compensatory damages such as litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorneys’ fees.

 The GAAIA would codify CAISI within the US Department of Commerce and place it at the center of the legislation’s federal standards and evaluation framework. Key obligations for CAISI under the GAIAA include: 
 Developing voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security and related evaluation work.

 Evaluating and monitoring activities tied to advanced AI systems.

 Supporting synthetic content detection tools.

 Administering the licensing regime for independent verification organizations that audit large frontier developers.

 US Federal: Unpacking the Great American AI Act

 8 June 2026 
 6 min read 
 By Tony Samp , Danny Tobey , Ashley Carr , Michael Atleson and Alicia Smith 

 LinkedIn 

 Facebook 

 Twitter 

 Saved to bookmarks . 

 Related topics

 At a glance

 Bipartisan lawmakers have released a 269-page discussion draft of the ‘Great American AI Act’, aiming to establish a comprehensive federal AI framework.

 The draft focuses on national uniformity, workforce impacts, and US leadership, including proposed federal pre-emption of certain state AI laws.

 It introduces transparency and oversight requirements for frontier AI developers, including reporting obligations and mandatory third-party audits.

 The bill includes whistleblower protections and potential civil penalties for non-compliance with key obligations.

 Stakeholder feedback is being sought before formal introduction, although early opposition has already emerged from some groups.

 On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence ( AI ) legislation titled the 'Great American AI Act' ( GAAIA ). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint  op-ed  in Bloomberg Law.

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “ policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties .”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and pre-emption:  ' Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough. '

 AI’s impact on the workforce:  ' Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.' 

 US leadership internationally:  ' By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.' 

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in  supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the  House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition  hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I).

 Workforce (Title II).

 Cybersecurity (Title III).

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV).

 Transparency in frontier AI models

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (section 113).

 Section 111

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a 'frontier AI framework ' focused on risk mitigation and the handling of 'catastrophic risk .' All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any 'critical safety incidents' to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation ( CAISI ).

 Section 112

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee 'independent verification organizations ( IVOs )' that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform 'audits and assessments .'

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s ' frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks .'

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General ( AG ) and state AGs. Referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding 'AI violations .' This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations ' related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence .'

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills

 All three sections borrow heavily from  recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is therefore the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another  recently enacted state law in Virginia  focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Notable pre-emption provisions

 Title I of the bill would pre-empt state laws and rules ' specifically regulating the development of' any AI model, where 'development' is broadly defined as ' acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment. ' The bill explains that the purpose of pre-emption is to allow the federal government to 'establish testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks .' Pre-emption would last for three years unless reauthorized.

 The bill makes clear that it does not apply post-deployment or pre-empt state laws or rules of 'general applicability.' Therefore, many AI-related state bills and laws would remain unaffected, such as laws regulating  companion bots  and  commercial chatbot interactions .

11 AI Bills Cleared Committee this Summer, But None Has Reached the House Floor 

 MILPITAS, Calif., Sept. 17, 2026 – Eleven bills carrying most of a bipartisan artificial intelligence package cleared the House Science Committee in July, and a separate bill setting safety rules for the most powerful AI systems could get a hearing in November, Rep. Jay Obernolte , R-Calif., said Thursday. 
 He said the pieces could be combined into a single bill eligible for a floor vote in December.

 Sign Up for FREE for Section A of '150 Years of American Telecommunications' 

 Sign up for FREE for Section A

 The package started as the Great American AI Act, a 269-page discussion draft Obernolte released with Rep. Lori Trahan , D-Mass., on June 4. Filed as one bill, it would have gone to as many as eight House committees, since it reaches federal AI research funding, cybersecurity, classroom curriculum, teacher training grants, workforce programs and safety rules for the largest models.
 11 bills, eight committees 
 The authors split the draft into 11 bills, each routed to the committee holding jurisdiction over its subject. The bills assigned to the House Science, Space and Technology Committee, which oversees federal research and technology programs, cleared it this summer. None has reached the House floor since.
 "It is a frustratingly slow process," Obernolte said at Tarana Wireless' Connecting Communities Summit , a broadband industry conference at the next-generation fixed wireless company's headquarters here.
 A federal consumer protection bill? 
 The safety provisions went to a different committee. The FRONTIER Act, introduced July 23, sits with the Energy and Commerce Committee, which writes communications and consumer protection law, and Obernolte said he hopes for a hearing when the House returns in November.
 The draft also carries the provision drawing the most opposition. Title I would preempt state laws governing how AI models are built, for three years unless Congress renews it, reaching what a developer does before deployment while leaving in place state rules on how AI gets used, along with privacy, consumer protection and civil rights statutes of general applicability.
 Trahan's office named two California laws the preemption would reach: AB 2013, which requires developers to publish summaries of their training data, and parts of SB 942, the state's AI content watermarking statute. Frontier safety laws in California, New York and Illinois would be federalized under the bill, according to her office.
 The bill aimed at catastrophic risk 
 What could replace those state rules sits in the bill aimed at catastrophic risk. The FRONTIER Act would set obligations according to what a system can do. 
 Companies training frontier models, the largest and most capable systems, would have to publish information about them, write plans for managing severe risks, report safety incidents and submit to review by independent verification organizations. Companies that only use AI tools built by other platforms would carry the lightest requirements.
 Obernolte represents California's 23rd District, running from the outer edge of Los Angeles County across the High Desert and the Mojave. He is a computer engineer with a graduate degree in artificial intelligence and chairs the House Task Force on AI.
 Across the aisle,  Rep. Sam Liccardo , D-Calif., named disclosure, transparency and third-party auditing as already drawing support from both the large AI developers and the safety advocates. That overlap is the part of the debate that could move quickly, he said.
 "I haven't seen a serious AI bill come to the floor yet," Liccardo said. "We need to get Jay's legislation done."
 Liccardo's own priority is catastrophic risk, including cyberattacks and AI systems that pursue objectives their operators did not intend. He represents California's 16th District, covering much of Silicon Valley including Palo Alto.
 The push for a floor vote 
 Congress repeated its social media pattern by waiting for documented harm before acting, Liccardo argued. He joined 106 other Democrats on Wednesday in asking Speaker Mike Johnson , R-La., to cancel a scheduled recess and vote on AI safeguards.
 The argument he hears against safety rules is competition with China. 
 That makes international engagement part of the safety question rather than separate from it, he said, and he plans to introduce legislation letting AI labs, universities and think tanks work with Chinese counterparts on shared safety metrics, testing protocols and verification methods. He also plans a bill in November giving communities leverage to negotiate with data center developers.
 Adoption hits a billion 
 OpenAI's chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane said more than 1 billion people use the company's products regularly, and that usage in rural areas is growing at about the same rate as in cities.
 The company runs a free training program, OpenAI Academy, with rural sessions built around agriculture. The tools are widely available already, Lehane said, and what differs is skill, since people who use them heavily produce about seven times what occasional users produce.
 That gap puts workforce training between an economy where the gains spread and one where they concentrate. Lehane proposed judging the result against a single number, the roughly $150,000 a year economists say a typical American family now needs for a middle-class life. The country could treat that as a national goal, he said, tracked the way the Federal Reserve tracks inflation and unemployment.

HTTP 200
Anthropic calls for pause of global AI development 

 skip to main content 

 Updated / Friday, 5 Jun 2026
 09:44

 Getty

 Anthropic has warned of AI systems that become capable of teaching themselves to get smarter without human help 

 Artificial intelligence company Anthropic has suggested a global pause on building the most powerful AI systems as the latest models are beginning to show signs they could escape human control.

 The San Francisco-based company, which makes the Claude family of AI models, said in a report that a worldwide slowdown in cutting-edge AI development would "likely be a good thing", but warned that if only one company stopped, rivals would simply race ahead.

 "We believe it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development to enable societal structures and alignment research to keep up with the advance of the technology," it said.

 Getting a real pause to work would mean multiple major AI companies in multiple countries, most notably the US and China, all agreeing to stop at the same time, under rules everyone could actually verify, Anthropic said.

 "Without a global coordination mechanism, companies and governments will have to make difficult decisions about safety while under competitive and geopolitical pressures," it said.

 The company has faced pushback from others in the industry, and officials in the White House, who say its focus on worst-case scenarios overstates the risks and amounts to a strategy for slowing rivals under the cover of safety concerns.

 Anthropic is led by former OpenAI employee Dario Amodei 

 Still, the White House has acknowledged the power of the company's Mythos model, which has not been made available to the general public due to its cybersecurity capabilities and is currently deployed only to a small number of vetted organizations.

 The proposal would face an uphill battle in Washington and Silicon Valley, where US officials and tech executives have repeatedly argued that any slowdown in AI development risks handing China a decisive strategic edge in what many see as the defining technology race of the century.

 US President Donald Trump, however, said he discussed the possibility of cooperating with China on AI safety issues during his recent visit to Beijing.

 Mr Trump also signed an executive order this week that allows the government 30 days to conduct a preliminary review of the most powerful US AI models before their release.

 'Human role narrowing', says Anthropic 

 Anthropic compared the problem to nuclear arms control treaties, but said it would be even harder to get a handle on, since AI training is far easier to hide than a missile silo, and the temptation to quietly keep going would be enormous.

 The company said it plans to bring together government officials, scientists, advocacy groups and competing AI firms in coming months to figure out how such a system could work.

 The call for coordination comes alongside internal data showing that AI is already dramatically speeding up the development of AI itself, Anthropic said.

 That acceleration creates a feedback loop that Anthropic warned could eventually lead to what researchers call "recursive self-improvement".

 That's the idea of an AI system that becomes capable of essentially teaching itself to get smarter, without much human help.

 "We are not there yet, and recursive self-improvement is not inevitable," the report said, while adding that it could arrive sooner than most governments and institutions are ready for.

 "The evidence suggests that the human role is narrowing at each step in the AI development process," the company said.

Over 200 state lawmakers urge Congress to oppose AI preemption in House proposal | The Hill - The Alliance for Secure AI Action State Lawmakers Push Back Against Federal AI Preemption Efforts 

 Skip to content 

 In the News 

 Home » Over 200 state lawmakers urge Congress to oppose AI preemption in House proposal | The Hill 

 The Hill:

 Over 200 state lawmakers urge Congress to oppose AI preemption in House proposal | The Hill

 June 17, 2026 

 By Miranda Nazzaro 

 Just over 200 state lawmakers from across the country are calling on members of the House and Senate to reject a proposal to preempt some state regulations of artificial intelligence for three years, citing the technology’s impact on kids, artists and creators and workers. 

 The letter, sent by 203 state lawmakers to Congress on Tuesday, said “we take seriously our responsibility to safeguard our constituents from AI harms to children, workers, artists and creators, families, and consumers.” 

 The preemption provision “would freeze a sweeping set of state laws and tie the hands of lawmakers at a moment of rapid technological transformation,” the lawmakers added in the letter, first shared with The Hill. 

 The letter, organized by the non-profits Americans for Responsible Innovation and The Alliance for Secure AI , refers to a measure included in a discussion draft of a national framework on AI being floated by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and  Lori Trahan  (D-Mass.) in the House. 

 The discussion draft proposes overriding state regulations that target AI model development for three years. This would not necessarily preempt state laws dictating how AI is used once released, as other proposals have suggested. 

 The draft “expressly does not preempt laws of general applicability, common law remedies, or laws regulating AI use or deployment,” a  summary of the draft  said. 

 The state lawmakers, made up of 104 Democrats, 98 Republicans and 1 independent, said the provision, even if limited, would apply to a “sweeping category of laws,” including measures about AI models trained on copyrighted materials, antidiscrimination training laws and private protection bills. 

 “Not only is the provision extremely broad as written, but the tech industry will almost certainly weaponize such a provision in court to strike down state measures not intended to fall within the scope of GAAIA,” they wrote. 

 The prospect of an AI preemption law has been in talks for more than a year, but Washington has largely stalled on getting anything across the finish line. The Senate came close to  passing a moratorium  on new state AI regulations last year, but it fell through at the last minute.

 State lawmakers have  long had concerns over preemption , along with some Republican governors willing to break with President Trump on the issue. 

 Tuesday’s letter compares the AI revolution to the emergence of social media, which has since faced growing backlash over the platform’s impacts on society, especially minors and young adults. 

 “The lessons of the social media era are clear: allowing Silicon Valley to write its own rulebook leaves industry unaccountable and leaves American families vulnerable to AI’s dangers,” the lawmakers wrote. 

 While the proposal was introduced in a bipartisan fashion, interparty and partisan agreements over AI regulation continue to stall legislation in Congress. 

 In the Senate, lawmaker and Tennessee gubernatorial candidate Sen.  Marsha Blackburn  (R-Tenn.) is leading negotiations with the White House to finalize text for an AI preemption package, her spokesperson told The Hill. 

 The package would include bills related to the protections of “kids, creators, and communities,” but it is not clear what the terms of preemption would be. 

 See More at The Hill 

 SHARE WITH YOUR NETWORK 

 Media Contact

 We welcome inquiries and interview requests from members of the media.  Please contact us for more information.

 Sign Up for Our Newsletter

 By signing up, you agree to receive email updates and communications from The Alliance for Secure AI Action.

October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for keeping the stakeholder record open while the House Energy and Commerce Committee considers the frontier provisions. This is the most serious bipartisan attempt yet to govern frontier AI, and it deserves a serious response. We offer ours in that spirit.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. We have one purpose: binding limits on frontier AI. We filed comments on the AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025, and we asked then for binding pre-deployment testing and for the states' right to act to be protected. Our members include parents, workers and congregations across the country, including in California and Massachusetts.

Our bottom line is straightforward: **we oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.** Testing and reporting rules do not make frontier AI safe. They describe it.

## 1. The draft names the danger, then does nothing about it

Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

Your own draft agrees with that diagnosis. Section 101 defines a "frontier model" as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations. Section 101 also defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk that a frontier model will contribute to the death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people, or to more than $1 billion in property damage, arising from a single incident. And the draft defines a "critical safety incident" to include loss of control of a frontier model.

You have written into the bill the recognition that these systems may escape their makers' control. What does the draft then do about it? Under Section 111, the developer has 15 days to tell the Director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). A report filed two weeks after a frontier model slips its leash is a record of the harm. It is not protection from the harm.

## 2. What the draft requires is paperwork

Strip away the 269 pages and the frontier provisions ask the largest developers to do four things.

Large frontier developers - those with more than $500 million in annual revenue - must write, implement and publish a "frontier AI framework" describing how they manage catastrophic risk (Section 111). All frontier developers must publish a transparency report before or alongside a new model, and report critical safety incidents to CAISI (Section 111). Large frontier developers must hire a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization to audit them twice a year (Section 112). And CAISI must publish voluntary guidelines and standards (Section 102).

That is the whole of it. No provision in the draft stops, slows, or conditions a single training run. The heaviest duty, the published framework, does not even take effect until a year after enactment.

The penalty for failing to do this paperwork is a civil fine of up to $1 million per violation, with each day counted as a separate violation, enforced by the Attorney General and, in some circumstances, by state attorneys general. The four largest cloud companies have guided to more than $700 billion in capital spending this year alone, overwhelmingly for AI infrastructure. For a large frontier developer, the draft's maximum penalty is a budget line.

## 3. The industry is making our argument for us

We are not asking you to accept our word for the risk. Take the word of a leading frontier developer.

On June 4, 2026, Anthropic wrote: "We believe it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development to enable societal structures and alignment research to keep up with the advance of the technology." The same company has kept its most capable model, Claude Mythos, out of general release because of the size of the capability jump, and deploys it only to vetted organizations. Executive Order 14409 of June 2, 2026 asks developers to voluntarily submit their most capable models for government review in the 30 days before release.

Anthropic also warned that "without a global coordination mechanism, companies and governments will have to make difficult decisions about safety while under competitive and geopolitical pressures." That is exactly right, and it is why a voluntary pause will not hold. Any single lab that pauses alone hands the frontier to its rivals. The only pause that survives contact with the market is one that is binding on everyone and enforced by the government. The draft before you is a record-keeping regime for a race that one of its leading runners says the world may need to stop.

## 4. What we ask you to write instead

**One: pause the frontier.** Impose an immediate moratorium on training any model above 10^26 FLOP - the very line you drew in Section 101 - until Congress certifies that systems above that line can be reliably controlled. The trigger for lifting the pause should be demonstrated control, certified by the government. Not a company's own assessment, published on its own website, redacted where it wishes.

**Two: wind down what is already deployed.** Frontier models already in service that cannot be independently certified should be withdrawn within 12 months. That includes open-weight releases: Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen. U.S. cloud providers should stop hosting and serving them. We are not pretending that copies already downloaded can be recalled. The obligation is to stop American companies amplifying the distribution, and to fund the detection and mitigation work that follows. Section 311's grants to maintainers of critical open-source software is the right instinct. Build on it.

**Three: hold executives personally accountable.** Criminal penalties should apply to executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the moratorium and the wind-down. In our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters, 66 percent said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm. A $1 million daily fine is a business expense. A criminal exposure is a decision that gets made in a boardroom.

**Four: strike Section 121.** The preemption provision would freeze state laws that regulate the development of AI models for three years, and would sweep in California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois' SB 315, California's AB 2013 and parts of SB 942 - according to the sponsors' own summary. California's law has been in force since January 1 of this year; New York's takes effect January 1, 2027. The draft would trade those live protections for a federal program that, under its own terms, switches off in three years unless Congress reauthorizes it. That is not a floor. It is a memo with an expiry date.

The politics here are not partisan. In June, 203 state legislators - 104 Democrats, 98 Republicans and one independent - wrote to Congress asking you to drop this provision. In our survey, 63 percent of voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

**Five: keep CAISI, but as the enforcement body for the pause.** Section 102 authorizes $100 million a year for CAISI to write voluntary standards, license auditors and monitor AI progress, with fee authority to collect money from the developers it oversees. We do not need a standards body to write guidance nobody is bound by, and we do not want the regulated industry paying the regulator's bills. Give CAISI the job that actually matters: verifying that no one is training above 10^26 FLOP, monitoring the large clusters where that training can only happen, running the certification tests that would let the pause be lifted, and enforcing the wind-down. If that is the assignment, we would support funding it well above $100 million a year.

## 5. What in the draft we would keep

- **Section 113, whistleblower protections.** We asked for these in our 2025 comments and we are glad to see them. They cannot be waived by contract, they cover contractors, and the remedies are real. Keep them, and extend them to anyone who reports a violation of the moratorium or the wind-down.
- **Section 251, WARN Act disclosures.** When AI is a substantial factor in a mass layoff, workers should be told, along with the share of jobs lost to it and what retraining was offered first. Our labor locals consider this the minimum honesty owed to a workforce.
- **Section 311, support for critical open-source maintainers.** Keep it, and use it to fund detection and mitigation for open-weight frontier models.
- **Section 122, GAO review, including model-weight security.** Keep it, make it recurring, and require a public report.
- **Incident reporting.** Keep the concept, but tighten it. New York's RAISE Act already requires reporting to the state within 72 hours. A 15-day federal clock is weaker than the state law it would displace.

## 6. On China

The objection we expect is competitiveness. Our answer: the race you cannot stop is not a race you are winning.

Between April and September of this year, eight of the ten leading Chinese model families released downloadable weights for a current flagship. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, released in July, is the largest open-weight model published to date. Chinese frontier capabilities are already on American laptops. Sprinting harder does not fence them off, and no American training run is made safer by a rival's.

What is scarce is not capability. It is control. The United States and China agreed this spring to launch an intergovernmental AI dialogue, and in September agreed a channel for handling AI incidents. That is the venue in which a verified, mutual pause can be built, and this Congress can set the standard for it. A country that can demonstrate its systems are under control will lead the next decade. A country that cannot is simply running faster toward the same cliff. Our members do not want their children to inherit that race.

## 7. Closing

We understand the draft has since been divided among committees, with its frontier provisions introduced as the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, now pending before Energy and Commerce. Every comment in this letter applies to that bill with equal force, and we would welcome the chance to make these points to the Committee.

We would rather help you write a bipartisan pause than fight a bipartisan bill. The coalition's members - parents, workers, people of faith and researchers - are ready to work with your staffs on text, and to bring our polling and our members to the Committee's attention.

Please treat these comments as part of the record for the discussion draft.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
[address / telephone / email to be inserted at transmission]

And it defines a "critical safety incident" to include "loss of control" of a frontier model.

You have written into law the recognition that these systems may get out of their makers' control. What does the draft then do? Under Section 111, a developer has 15 days to tell CAISI about it. A report filed two weeks after a frontier model escapes oversight is a record of the harm, not a protection from it. [short]

No provision in the draft stops, slows, or conditions a single training run. ...

## 3. The industry is telling you the same thing

Anthropic, one of the three largest frontier developers, published on June 4, 2026: "We believe it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development to enable societal structures and alignment research to keep up with the advance of the technology." The same company withheld its most capable model, Claude Mythos, from general release because of the size of the capability jump. **2. Wind down what is already deployed.** ... within 12 months ... including open-weight releases: Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen. Section 311's grants to maintainers of critical open-source software is the right instinct; build on it.

...

... offer to work together; the FRONTIER Act at E&C — our comments apply with full force to H.R. 9925 ... invite meeting.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director, Frontier Restraint Coalition

{"content": "# GAAIA discussion draft - FRC asks by section

**Work order:** FRC-POL-2026-062 (draft, 16 Oct 2026; for ED review Fri 23 Oct)
**Overall position:** OPPOSE the draft as written. Replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium. Strike preemption.
**Source of positions:** FRC Messaging Guide v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026). Section numbers from the 4 June 2026 discussion draft (269 pp.) and the sponsors' section-by-section summary.

## A. Provisions in the draft

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 101 - Definitions.** "Frontier model" = foundation model trained with more than 10^26 operations; "frontier developer" (>$50M revenue), "large frontier developer" (>$500M); defines "catastrophic risk" and "critical safety incident." | **Support the threshold; oppose what follows it.** | Keep the 10^26 definition and make it the moratorium line; require an annual rulemaking so the line holds if capability arrives at lower compute. | The draft names the line that cannot be crossed safely, then lets developers cross it and file a report. |
| **Sec. 102 - CAISI** codified at Commerce: voluntary guidelines and standards, evaluation, monitoring of AI progress, IVO licensing; $100M/yr FY2027-2029 plus fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers. | **Oppose as drafted.** | Rewrite CAISI's charter as the enforcement body for the pause: verify training runs at or above 10^26 FLOP, monitor the large clusters, run certification testing, enforce the wind-down. Strip or ring-fence the fee authority; fund it above $100M if that is the job. | $100 million a year for voluntary guidance buys a well-documented race, not a safe one - and the industry should not pay the regulator's bills. |
| **Sec. 111 - Frontier AI frameworks and transparency reports** (large frontier developers publish and follow a framework within one year of enactment; all frontier developers publish transparency reports before or with deployment). | **Oppose.** | Replace with the moratorium (see Part B). If any transparency duty survives, keep the transparency report only as a complement to the pause, not a substitute for it. | A company's own published plan, redacted where it wishes, is a press release - not proof that a frontier model is under control. |
| **Sec. 111 - Critical safety incident reporting**: 15 days to the CAISI Director; 24 hours to law enforcement only where there is imminent risk of death or serious injury. | **Oppose the timelines; support the concept.** | 24 hours to the regulator for any critical safety incident, including loss of control; publish a summary within 30 days where safe. | New York's RAISE Act already requires 72-hour reporting; a federal bill that preempts it should not run a 15-day clock. |
| **Secs. 111-112 - Civil penalty**: up to $1M per violation, each day a separate violation, enforced by the AG and (in some circumstances) state AGs, plus injunctions. | **Oppose as the only deterrent.** | Keep civil penalties for reporting failures; add criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause or wind-down. | 66% of voters back criminal penalties when AI causes mass harm; a $1M daily fine is a budget line for firms whose cloud backers are spending $700B+ this year. |
| **Sec. 112 - IVO audits and assessments**: CAISI licenses auditors; large frontier developers are audited semi-annually and on request; auditors are immune from claims arising from models they audit. | **Oppose.** | Repoint the IVO regime at verifying the pause and certifying the wind-down; delete the IVO immunity. | Twice-a-year audits of paperwork, by firms immune from the consequences, are not verification of control. |

{"content": "# Staff Q&A - GAAIA discussion draft (anticipated questions)

**Work order:** FRC-POL-2026-062 (draft, 16 Oct 2026). For ED review Fri 23 Oct; for use in Hill meetings. Answers are each within 120 words; keep the plain-language framing if staff paraphrase.

---

**1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?**

Because reporting describes harm after the fact, and CAISI's standards are voluntary. The draft itself defines "catastrophic risk" as the death of or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage, from a single incident - and it defines a critical safety incident to include loss of control of a model. Section 111 then gives the developer 15 days to tell CAISI. Section 102 tells CAISI to publish voluntary guidelines. Section 112 audits the paperwork twice a year. Nothing in the bill slows a training run. Our members are parents, workers and congregations. They do not want a better record of the accident. They want the pause, the wind-down, and criminal liability when executives knowingly break the rules.

---

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?**

Dropping Section 121 is necessary, but it is not sufficient. We would still oppose a frontier title that asks only for published plans, transparency reports and twice-yearly audits, because none of that slows the race. Our support follows two changes: strike Section 121 entirely, and put the moratorium in its place - no training above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies control, a 12-month wind-down of uncertified models, and criminal liability for knowing violations. On the window itself: shortening it makes the trade worse, not better. The federal duties start a year after enactment and sunset in three unless reauthorized, so states would lose live protections for a program that may not exist. Sixty-three percent of voters in our August poll want states free to act.

---

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?**

Racing does not fence China's capabilities in, because they are already out. Between April and September, eight of the ten leading Chinese model families released downloadable weights for current flagships, and Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 - the largest open-weight model published to date - dropped in July. Those models are on American laptops now. What is scarce is not capability; it is control. The United States and China agreed this spring to an intergovernmental AI dialogue and, in September, to a channel for handling AI incidents. That is the venue for a verified, mutual pause, and this Congress can set the standard for it. The country that can show its systems stay under control leads the next decade. The one that cannot is running faster toward the same cliff.

---

**4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?**

$100 million a year is a rounding error next to the $700 billion-plus the four largest cloud firms are spending this year on AI infrastructure. Our view of the level depends on the assignment. As drafted, the money buys voluntary guidelines, licensing of auditors and monitoring - a standards shop. We would support funding well above $100 million if CAISI becomes the enforcement body for the pause: verifying that nobody trains above 10^26 FLOP, monitoring the large clusters where that training can happen, running certification testing, and enforcing the wind-down. On authorities, we would strike the fee authority in Section 102. A regulator funded by fees from the developers it oversees is a capture risk. That work should be appropriations-funded.
", "path": "/workspace/out/staff_qa.md"}

<!-- FRC-POL-2026-062 | DRAFT v1 for Executive Director sign-off, Fri 23 Oct 2026.
     Not for transmission from this workspace. Update the dateline when filed to
     GAAIA@mail.house.gov. Word count: ~1,960. -->

October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for keeping the stakeholder record open while the House Energy and Commerce Committee considers the frontier provisions. This is the most serious bipartisan attempt yet to govern frontier AI, and it deserves a serious response. We offer ours in that spirit.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. We have one purpose: binding limits on frontier AI. We filed comments on the AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025, and we asked then for binding pre-deployment testing and for the states' right to act to be protected. Our members include parents, workers and congregations across the country, including in California and Massachusetts.

Our bottom line is straightforward: **we oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.** Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

## 1. The draft names the danger, then does nothing about it

Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

Your own draft agrees with that diagnosis. Section 101 defines a "frontier model" as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations. Section 101 also defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of death or serious injury to more than 50 people, or of more than $1 billion in property damage, arising from a single incident. And the draft defines a "critical safety incident" to include loss of control of a frontier model.

You have written into the bill the recognition that these systems may escape their makers' control. What does the draft then do about it? Under Section 111, the developer has 15 days to tell the Director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). A report filed two weeks after a frontier model slips its leash is a record of the harm. It is not protection from the harm.

## 2. What the draft requires is paperwork

Strip away the 269 pages and the frontier provisions ask the largest developers to do four things.

Large frontier developers - those with more than $500 million in annual revenue - must write, implement and publish a "frontier AI framework" describing how they manage catastrophic risk (Section 111). All frontier developers must publish a transparency report before or alongside a new model, and report critical safety incidents to CAISI (Section 111). Large frontier developers must hire a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization to audit them twice a year (Section 112). And CAISI must publish voluntary guidelines and standards (Section 102).

That is the whole of it. No provision in the draft stops, slows, or conditions a single training run. The heaviest duty, the published framework, does not even take effect until a year after enactment.

The penalty for failing to do this paperwork is a civil fine of up to $1 million per violation, with each day counted as a separate violation, enforced by the Attorney General and, in some circumstances, by state attorneys general. The four largest cloud companies have guided to more than $700 billion in capital spending this year alone, overwhelmingly for AI infrastructure. For a large frontier developer, the draft's maximum penalty is a budget line.

## 3. The industry is making our argument for us

We are not asking you to accept our word for the risk. Take the word of a leading frontier developer.

On June 4, 2026, Anthropic wrote: "We believe it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development to enable societal structures and alignment research to keep up with the advance of the technology." The same company has kept its most capable model, Claude Mythos, out of general release because of the size of the capability jump, and deploys it only to vetted organizations. Executive Order 14409 of June 2, 2026 asks developers to voluntarily submit their most capable models for government review in the 30 days before release.

Anthropic also warned that "without a global coordination mechanism, companies and governments will have to make difficult decisions about safety while under competitive and geopolitical pressures." That is exactly right, and it is why a voluntary pause will not hold. Any single lab that pauses alone hands the frontier to its rivals. The only pause that survives contact with the market is one that is binding on everyone and enforced by the government. The draft before you is a record-keeping regime for a race that one of its leading runners says the world may need to stop.

## 4. What we ask you to write instead

**One: pause the frontier.** Impose an immediate moratorium on training any model above 10^26 FLOP - the very line you drew in Section 101, which already counts later fine-tuning and substantial modification toward the threshold - until Congress certifies that systems above that line can be reliably controlled. The trigger for lifting the pause should be demonstrated control, certified by the government. Not a company's own assessment, published on its own website, redacted where it wishes. That is what 74 percent of voters told us they want in August: companies made to prove their most powerful systems are safe before they are released.

**Two: wind down what is already deployed.** Frontier models already in service that cannot be independently certified should be withdrawn within 12 months. That includes open-weight releases: Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen. U.S. cloud providers should stop hosting and serving them. We are not pretending that copies already downloaded can be recalled. The obligation is to stop American companies amplifying the distribution, and to fund the detection and mitigation work that follows. Section 311's grants to maintainers of critical open-source software is the right instinct. Build on it.

**Three: hold executives personally accountable.** Criminal penalties should apply to executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the moratorium and the wind-down. In our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters, 66 percent said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm. A $1 million daily fine is a business expense. A criminal exposure is a decision that gets made in a boardroom.

**Four: strike Section 121.** The preemption provision would freeze state laws that regulate the development of AI models for three years, and would sweep in California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois' SB 315, California's AB 2013 and parts of SB 942 - according to the sponsors' own summary. California's law has been in force since January 1 of this year; New York's takes effect January 1, 2027. The draft would trade those live protections for a federal program that, under its own terms, switches off in three years unless Congress reauthorizes it. That is not a floor. It is a memo with an expiry date.

The politics here are not partisan. In June, 203 state legislators - 104 Democrats, 98 Republicans and one independent - wrote to Congress asking you to drop this provision. In our survey, 63 percent of voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

**Five: keep CAISI, but as the enforcement body for the pause.** Section 102 authorizes $100 million a year for CAISI to write voluntary standards, license auditors and monitor AI progress, with fee authority to collect money from the developers it oversees. We do not need a standards body to write guidance nobody is bound by, and we do not want the regulated industry paying the regulator's bills. Give CAISI the job that actually matters: verifying that no one is training above 10^26 FLOP, monitoring the large clusters where that training can only happen, running the certification tests that would let the pause be lifted, and enforcing the wind-down. If that is the assignment, we would support funding it well above $100 million a year.

## 5. What in the draft we would keep

- **Section 113, whistleblower protections.** We asked for these in our 2025 comments and we are glad to see them. They cannot be waived by contract, they cover contractors, and the remedies are real. Keep them, and extend them to anyone who reports a violation of the moratorium or the wind-down.
- **Section 251, WARN Act disclosures.** When AI is a substantial factor in a mass layoff, workers should be told, along with the share of jobs lost to it and what retraining was offered first. Our labor locals consider this the minimum honesty owed to a workforce.
- **Section 311, support for critical open-source maintainers.** Keep it, and use it to fund detection and mitigation for open-weight frontier models.
- **Section 122, GAO review, including model-weight security.** Keep it, make it recurring, and require a public report.
- **Incident reporting.** Keep the concept, but tighten it. New York's RAISE Act already requires reporting to the state within 72 hours. A 15-day federal clock is weaker than the state law it would displace.

## 6. On China

The objection we expect is competitiveness. Our answer: the race you cannot stop is not a race you are winning.

Between April and September of this year, eight of the ten leading Chinese model families released downloadable weights for a current flagship. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, released in July, is the largest open-weight model published to date. Chinese frontier capabilities are already on American laptops. Sprinting harder does not fence them off, and no American training run is made safer by a rival's.

What is scarce is not capability. It is control. The United States and China agreed this spring to launch an intergovernmental AI dialogue, and in September agreed a channel for handling AI incidents. That is the venue in which a verified, mutual pause can be built, and this Congress can set the standard for it. A country that can demonstrate its systems are under control will lead the next decade. A country that cannot is simply running faster toward the same cliff. Our members do not want their children to inherit that race.

## 7. Closing

We understand the draft has since been divided among committees, with its frontier provisions introduced as the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, now pending before Energy and Commerce. Every comment in this letter applies to that bill with equal force, and we would welcome the chance to make these points to the Committee.

We would rather help you write a bipartisan pause than fight a bipartisan bill. The coalition's members - parents, workers, people of faith and researchers - are ready to work with your staffs on text, and to bring our polling and our members to the Committee's attention.

Please treat these comments as part of the record for the discussion draft.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

messages.content:
# GAAIA discussion draft - FRC asks by section

**Work order:** FRC-POL-2026-062 (draft, 16 Oct 2026; for ED review Fri 23 Oct)
**Overall position:** OPPOSE the draft as written. Replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium. Strike preemption.
**Source of positions:** FRC Messaging Guide v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026). Section numbers from the 4 June 2026 discussion draft (269 pp.) and the sponsors' section-by-section summary.
**Note for the policy team:** this closes out the "section numbers - TODO" flag in the 2 Oct staff summary; all section cites below were checked against the sponsors' section-by-section and the draft text.

## A. Provisions in the draft

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 101 - Definitions.** "Frontier model" = foundation model trained with more than 10^26 operations; "frontier developer" (>$50M revenue), "large frontier developer" (>$500M); defines "catastrophic risk" and "critical safety incident." | **Support the threshold; oppose what follows it.** | Keep the 10^26 definition and make it the moratorium line; require an annual rulemaking so the line holds if capability arrives at lower compute. | The draft names the line that cannot be crossed safely, then lets developers cross it and file a report. |
| **Sec. 102 - CAISI** codified at Commerce: voluntary guidelines and standards, evaluation, monitoring of AI progress, IVO licensing; $100M/yr FY2027-2029 plus fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers. | **Oppose as drafted.** | Rewrite CAISI's charter as the enforcement body for the pause: verify training runs at or above 10^26 FLOP, monitor the large clusters, run certification testing, enforce the wind-down. Strip or ring-fence the fee authority; fund it above $100M if that is the job. | $100 million a year for voluntary guidance buys a well-documented race, not a safe one - and the industry should not pay the regulator's bills. |
| **Sec. 111 - Frontier AI frameworks and transparency reports** (large frontier developers publish and follow a framework within one year of enactment; all frontier developers publish transparency reports before or with deployment). | **Oppose.** | Replace with the moratorium (see Part B). If any transparency duty survives, keep the transparency report only as a complement to the pause, not a substitute for it. | A company's own published plan, redacted where it wishes, is a press release - not proof that a frontier model is under control. |
| **Sec. 111 - Critical safety incident reporting**: 15 days to the CAISI Director; 24 hours to law enforcement only where there is imminent risk of death or serious injury. | **Oppose the timelines; support the concept.** | 24 hours to the regulator for any critical safety incident, including loss of control; publish a public summary within 30 days, redacted only where necessary. | New York's RAISE Act already requires 72-hour reporting; a federal bill that preempts it should not run a 15-day clock. |
| **Secs. 111-112 - Civil penalty**: up to $1M per violation, each day a separate violation, enforced by the AG and (in some circumstances) state AGs, plus injunctions. | **Oppose as the only deterrent.** | Keep civil penalties for reporting failures; add criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause or wind-down. | 66% of voters back criminal penalties when AI causes mass harm; a $1M daily fine is a budget line for firms whose cloud backers are spending $700B+ this year. |
| **Sec. 112 - IVO audits and assessments**: CAISI licenses auditors; large frontier developers are audited semi-annually and on request; auditors are immune from claims arising from models they audit. | **Oppose.** | Repoint the IVO regime at verifying the pause and certifying the wind-down; delete the IVO immunity. | Twice-a-year audits of paperwork, by firms immune from the consequences, are not verification of control. |
| **Secs. 111-112 - Three-year sunset** of the frontier provisions unless Congress reauthorizes. | **Oppose.** | If the frontier provisions are replaced by the moratorium, no sunset on the pause itself; Congress lifts it by certifying control, not by default. | A safety regime that switches itself off is a floor that disappears. |
| **Sec. 113 - Whistleblower protections**: non-waivable, covers employees and independent contractors, double back pay plus costs and fees. | **Support.** | Keep, and extend to anyone reporting a violation of the pause or the wind-down. | We asked for this in 2025; it is the strongest part of the draft. |
| **Sec. 121 - Preemption** of state and local laws "specifically regulating the development" of AI models, for three years unless reauthorized. | **Oppose. Strike it.** | Delete Sec. 121. (Fallback if sponsors insist: an express savings clause for state frontier-safety statutes - CA SB 53, NY RAISE, IL SB 315 - and disclosure laws such as CA AB 2013 and SB 942.) | The sponsors' own summary lists the state laws this would federalize; Congress should add to them, not delete them. |
| **Sec. 121(c) - Savings clause**: preserves laws of general applicability, common-law remedies, use/deployment regulation, and state authority granted by the Act; state AGs may opt in to reports. | **Oppose as a fix.** | Do not rely on the savings clause; it is the same preemption with a narrower blade. | 203 state legislators (104 D, 98 R, 1 I) and 63% of voters in our poll want states free to act. |
| **Sec. 122 - GAO review** of federal agency AI adoption, including model-weight security. | **Support.** | Keep; make it recurring and require a public report. | Independent review of how the government itself secures weights is cheap and useful. |
| **Sec. 251 - WARN Act disclosures** when AI is a substantial factor in a qualifying mass layoff (type of AI, share of losses, prior retraining). | **Support.** | Keep as drafted. | Workers are owed a straight answer about why the jobs went. |
| **Sec. 311 - Grants to critical open-source maintainers**; large frontier developers must give maintainers model access. | **Support.** | Keep, and direct a share of the funding to detection and mitigation tooling for open-weight frontier models. | The open-weight wind-down will need people who can find and blunt these models in the wild. |
| **Secs. 301, 141 and other non-frontier provisions** (Cybersecurity Act reauthorization to 2035; government-AI platform "jawboning" study). | **No position.** | None. | Outside the coalition's remit on frontier limits. |

## B. What we ask the sponsors to add

| New provision (not in the draft) | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Frontier moratorium.** Immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP. | **Support - this is our principal ask.** | Add a new subtitle replacing Secs. 111-112; the pause ends only when Congress certifies such systems can be reliably controlled. | No developer can show its most capable systems are controllable; stopping the race is the only lever that works. |
| **Wind-down of deployed frontier models.** Withdrawal within 12 months of models that cannot be independently certified. | **Support.** | Add withdrawal duties for developers and a hosting/serving ban for U.S. cloud providers; include open-weight releases (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen). | Copies already downloaded cannot be recalled, but U.S. companies can stop amplifying the distribution. |
| **Executive criminal liability** for knowingly training or serving frontier models in violation of the pause or wind-down. | **Support.** | Add to the enforcement subtitle alongside civil penalties. | Fines are a cost of doing business; personal exposure changes decisions. |
| **Control certification standard** for lifting the pause. | **Support.** | Require CAISI to set the evidentiary standard and Congress to vote on the certification. | "Safely controlled" has to mean something before the race resumes. |

<!-- FRC-POL-2026-062 | DRAFT v1 for Executive Director sign-off, Fri 23 Oct 2026.
