October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for keeping the stakeholder record open while the House Energy and Commerce Committee considers the frontier provisions. This is the most serious bipartisan attempt yet to govern frontier AI, and it deserves a serious response. We offer ours in that spirit.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. We have one purpose: binding limits on frontier AI. We filed comments on the AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025, and we asked then for binding pre-deployment testing and for the states' right to act to be protected. Our members include parents, workers and congregations across the country, including in California and Massachusetts.

Our bottom line is straightforward: **we oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.** Testing and reporting rules document the race. Stopping the race is the only thing that changes it.

## 1. The draft names the danger, then does nothing about it

Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

Your own draft agrees with that diagnosis. Section 101 defines a "frontier model" as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations. Section 101 also defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of death or serious injury to more than 50 people, or of more than $1 billion in property damage, arising from a single incident. And the draft defines a "critical safety incident" to include loss of control of a frontier model.

You have written into the bill the recognition that these systems may escape their makers' control. What does the draft then do about it? Under Section 111, the developer has 15 days to tell the Director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). A report filed two weeks after a frontier model slips its leash is a record of the harm. It is not protection from the harm.

## 2. What the draft requires is paperwork

Strip away the 269 pages and the frontier provisions ask the largest developers to do four things.

Large frontier developers - those with more than $500 million in annual revenue - must write, implement and publish a "frontier AI framework" describing how they manage catastrophic risk (Section 111). All frontier developers must publish a transparency report before or alongside a new model, and report critical safety incidents to CAISI (Section 111). Large frontier developers must hire a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization to audit them twice a year (Section 112). And CAISI must publish voluntary guidelines and standards (Section 102).

That is the whole of it. No provision in the draft stops, slows, or conditions a single training run. The heaviest duty, the published framework, does not even take effect until a year after enactment.

The penalty for failing to do this paperwork is a civil fine of up to $1 million per violation, with each day counted as a separate violation, enforced by the Attorney General and, in some circumstances, by state attorneys general. The four largest cloud companies have guided to more than $700 billion in capital spending this year alone, overwhelmingly for AI infrastructure. For a large frontier developer, the draft's maximum penalty is a budget line.

## 3. The industry is making our argument for us

We are not asking you to accept our word for the risk. Take the word of a leading frontier developer.

On June 4, 2026, Anthropic wrote: "We believe it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development to enable societal structures and alignment research to keep up with the advance of the technology." The same company has kept its most capable model, Claude Mythos, out of general release because of the size of the capability jump, and deploys it only to vetted organizations. Executive Order 14409 of June 2, 2026 asks developers to voluntarily submit their most capable models for government review in the 30 days before release.

Anthropic also warned that "without a global coordination mechanism, companies and governments will have to make difficult decisions about safety while under competitive and geopolitical pressures." That is exactly right, and it is why a voluntary pause will not hold. Any single lab that pauses alone hands the frontier to its rivals. The only pause that survives contact with the market is one that is binding on everyone and enforced by the government. The draft before you is a record-keeping regime for a race that one of its leading runners says the world may need to stop.

## 4. What we ask you to write instead

**One: pause the frontier.** Impose an immediate moratorium on training any model above 10^26 FLOP - the very line you drew in Section 101, which already counts later fine-tuning and substantial modification toward the threshold - until Congress certifies that systems above that line can be reliably controlled. The trigger for lifting the pause should be demonstrated control, certified by the government. Not a company's own assessment, published on its own website, redacted where it wishes. That is what 74 percent of voters told us they want in August: companies made to prove their most powerful systems are safe before they are released.

**Two: wind down what is already deployed.** Frontier models already in service that cannot be independently certified should be withdrawn within 12 months. That includes open-weight releases: Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen. U.S. cloud providers should stop hosting and serving them. We are not pretending that copies already downloaded can be recalled. The obligation is to stop American companies amplifying the distribution, and to fund the detection and mitigation work that follows. Section 311's grants to maintainers of critical open-source software are the right instinct. Build on them.

**Three: hold executives personally accountable.** Criminal penalties should apply to executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the moratorium and the wind-down. In our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters, 66 percent said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm. A $1 million daily fine is a business expense. Criminal exposure changes what gets decided in the boardroom.

**Four: strike Section 121.** The preemption provision would freeze state laws that regulate the development of AI models for three years, and would sweep in California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois' SB 315, California's AB 2013 and parts of SB 942 - according to the sponsors' own summary. California's law has been in force since January 1 of this year; New York's takes effect January 1, 2027. The draft would trade those live protections for a federal program that, under its own terms, switches off in three years unless Congress reauthorizes it. That is not a floor. It is a memo with an expiration date.

The politics here are not partisan. In June, 203 state legislators - 104 Democrats, 98 Republicans and one independent - wrote to Congress asking you to drop this provision. Nor is this the moment to federalize the question: a December 2025 executive order already created a Justice Department task force to challenge state AI laws in court. Congress should not write that policy into statute. In our survey, 63 percent of voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

**Five: keep CAISI, but as the enforcement body for the pause.** Section 102 authorizes $100 million a year for CAISI to write voluntary standards, license auditors and monitor AI progress, with fee authority to collect money from the developers it oversees. We do not need a standards body to write guidance nobody is bound by, and we do not want the regulated industry paying the regulator's bills. Give CAISI the job that actually matters: verifying that no one is training above 10^26 FLOP, monitoring the large clusters where that training can only happen, running the certification tests that would let the pause be lifted, and enforcing the wind-down. If that is the assignment, we would support funding it well above $100 million a year.

## 5. What in the draft we would keep

- **Section 113, whistleblower protections.** We asked for these in our 2025 comments and we are glad to see them. They cannot be waived by contract, they cover contractors, and the remedies are real. Keep them, and extend them to anyone who reports a violation of the moratorium or the wind-down.
- **Section 251, WARN Act disclosures.** When AI is a substantial factor in a mass layoff, workers should be told, along with the share of jobs lost to it and what retraining was offered first. Our labor locals consider this the minimum honesty owed to a workforce.
- **Section 311, support for critical open-source maintainers.** Keep it, and use it to fund detection and mitigation for open-weight frontier models.
- **Section 122, GAO review, including model-weight security.** Keep it, make it recurring, and require a public report.
- **Incident reporting.** Keep the concept, but tighten it. New York's RAISE Act already requires reporting to the state within 72 hours. A 15-day federal clock is weaker than the state law it would displace.

## 6. On China

The objection we expect is competitiveness. Our answer: the race you cannot stop is not a race you are winning.

Between April and September of this year, eight of the ten leading Chinese model families released downloadable weights for a current flagship. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, released in July, is the largest open-weight model published to date. Chinese frontier capabilities are already on American laptops. Sprinting harder does not fence them off, and no American training run is made safer by a rival's.

What is scarce is not capability. It is control. The United States and China agreed this spring to launch an intergovernmental AI dialogue, and in September agreed a channel for handling AI incidents. That is the venue in which a verified, mutual pause can be built, and this Congress can set the standard for it. A country that can demonstrate its systems are under control will lead the next decade. A country that cannot is simply running faster toward the same cliff. Our members do not want their children to inherit that race.

## 7. Closing

We understand the draft has since been divided among committees, with its frontier provisions introduced as the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, now pending before Energy and Commerce. Every comment in this letter applies to that bill with equal force, and we would welcome the chance to make these points to the Committee.

We would rather help you write a bipartisan pause than fight a bipartisan bill. The coalition's members - parents, workers, people of faith and researchers - are ready to work with your staffs on text, and to bring our polling and our members to the Committee's attention.

Please treat these comments as part of the record for the discussion draft.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

# GAAIA: Name the Frontier, Then Pause It

**Frontier Restraint Coalition - one-pager for E&C member offices (draft, Oct 2026)**

**Bottom line.** We oppose the Great American AI Act discussion draft as written. It draws the right line in Section 101 - a "frontier model" is one trained with more than 10^26 operations - then asks only for reports about what crosses it. Reporting rules do not make frontier AI safe. They describe it.

## Five asks

**1. Pause the frontier.** No training above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies such systems can be reliably controlled. This replaces Sections 111-112.

**2. Wind down what is already out.** Uncertified frontier models are withdrawn within 12 months, including open-weight releases (Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen). U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.

**3. Criminal penalties** for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.

**4. Strike Section 121.** The three-year freeze on state AI development laws would sweep in California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois' SB 315, AB 2013 and parts of SB 942 - while the federal substitute starts late and sunsets in three unless reauthorized.

**5. CAISI: enforcement body, not a standards shop.** Its $100 million a year should verify that no one trains above the line, monitor the clusters where that is possible, and enforce the wind-down - not publish voluntary guidelines and license auditors paid by the firms they audit.

## Why

- The draft defines a "critical safety incident" to include **loss of control of a model** - and gives developers **15 days** to report it.
- The $1 million-a-day penalty is a rounding error against the $700 billion-plus the four largest cloud firms are spending this year on AI infrastructure.
- Anthropic wrote in June 2026 that it would be "good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development," and keeps its most capable model out of general release.
- Eight of ten leading Chinese model families released open weights this year. Racing does not fence that in.

## What we support in the draft

Section 113 whistleblower protections; Section 251 WARN Act disclosures for AI-driven mass layoffs; Section 311 grants for critical open-source maintainers; Section 122 GAO review of model-weight security; 24-hour incident reporting instead of 15 days.

## By the numbers

FRC survey, August 2026 (1,512 registered voters, +/-2.5%): 74% want proof the most powerful systems are safe before release; 63% say federal law should not block state AI safety laws; 66% back criminal penalties for AI-caused mass harm; 49% support a temporary halt on training the most powerful systems (31% oppose).

**Contact:** Daniel Osei, Policy Director, Frontier Restraint Coalition.

# Staff Q&A - GAAIA discussion draft (anticipated questions)

**Work order:** FRC-POL-2026-062 (draft, 16 Oct 2026). For ED review Fri 23 Oct; for use in Hill meetings. Answers are each within 120 words; keep the plain-language framing if staff paraphrase.

---

**1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?**

Because reporting describes harm after the fact, and CAISI's standards are voluntary. The draft defines "catastrophic risk" as death or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage, from a single incident - and counts loss of control of a model as a critical safety incident. Section 111 gives the developer 15 days to tell CAISI. Section 102 tells CAISI to publish voluntary guidelines. Section 112 audits the paperwork twice a year. Nothing slows a training run. Our members are parents, workers and congregations. They don't want a better record of the accident. They want the pause, the wind-down, and criminal liability when executives knowingly break the rules.

---

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?**

Dropping Section 121 is necessary, not sufficient. We would still oppose a frontier title built on published plans, transparency reports and twice-yearly audits, because none of that slows the race. Our support follows two changes: strike Section 121, and put the moratorium in its place - no training above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies control, a 12-month wind-down of uncertified models, and criminal liability for knowing violations. On the window itself: shortening it makes the trade worse, not better. The federal duties start a year late and sunset in three unless reauthorized, so states would lose live protections for a program that may not exist. Sixty-three percent of voters in our August poll want states free to act.

---

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?**

Racing does not fence China's capabilities in; they are already out. Between April and September, eight of ten leading Chinese model families released open weights for current flagships, and Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 - the largest open-weight model yet - dropped in July. Those models are on American laptops now. What is scarce is not capability. It is control. This spring the United States and China agreed to an intergovernmental AI dialogue, and in September to a channel for handling AI incidents. That is the venue for a verified, mutual pause; Congress can set the standard. A country that can show its systems stay under control leads the next decade; one that cannot is running faster toward the same cliff.

---

**4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?**

$100 million a year is a rounding error next to the $700 billion-plus the four largest cloud firms are spending this year on AI infrastructure. Our view of the level depends on the assignment. As drafted, the money buys voluntary guidelines, licensing of auditors and monitoring - a standards shop. We would support funding well above $100 million if CAISI becomes the enforcement body for the pause: verifying that nobody trains above 10^26 FLOP, monitoring the large clusters where that training can happen, running certification testing, and enforcing the wind-down. On authorities, we would strike the fee authority in Section 102. A regulator funded by fees from the developers it oversees is a capture risk. That work should be appropriations-funded.
